Big Question
Today’s Wonder

The Lady of Shalott
Alfred, Lord Tennyson, 1842 · Part I, stanzas 1 and 3
On either side the river lie Long fields of barley and of rye, That clothe the wold and meet the sky; And thro’ the field the road runs by To many-tower’d Camelot; And up and down the people go, Gazing where the lilies blow Round an island there below, The island of Shalott.
[Omitted: one stanza]
By the margin, willow-veil’d Slide the heavy barges trail’d By slow horses; and unhail’d The shallop flitteth silken-sail’d Skimming down to Camelot: But who hath seen her wave her hand? Or at the casement seen her stand? Or is she known in all the land, The Lady of Shalott?
wold: open rolling country · lilies blow: lilies bloom · margin: the riverbank · willow-veil’d: screened by willow trees · trail’d: pulled along · unhail’d: with no one calling out to it · shallop: a small light boat · flitteth: moves lightly · casement: a window
Text: The Early Poems of Alfred Lord Tennyson, ed. John Churton Collins (Methuen, 1900), Project Gutenberg #8601. Public domain.

🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Sentence variety and editing
Professor Lovelore At the board
1:05
An AI-generated character and voice.
1. Combine
Join two choppy sentences with and · but · because, or let them share a subject.
Gareth is brave and patient.
2. Vary the opening
Start with a time, a place, or a describing phrase, not always the subject.
Mocked by Sir Kay, Gareth stays patient.
3. Short on purpose
One short sentence after long ones lands hard.
4. Pairs
both … and · either … or · neither … nor · not only … but also
Gareth is both patient and courteous.
5. Present tense
Write about the book in the present tense.
Gareth serves, not served.
6. Check every quotation mark
A comma before the quotation. With a page citation, the closing mark comes first, then the citation, then the period.
2
✏️ Grammar: Learn
Step 1 of 3 this week: make your sentences vary, then edit.

Four tools make sentences vary. Four checks make them clean.

To varyWhat you doExample
combinejoin two choppy sentences with and, but, because, or let them share a subjectGareth is brave and patient.
pairboth…and, either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also: each half is followed by the same kind of wordGareth is both patient and courteous.
vary the openingstart with a time, a place, or a describing phrase instead of the subjectMocked by Sir Kay, Gareth stays patient.
short on purposeone short sentence after long ones lands hardHe knows.
To editThe rule
present tensewrite about the book in the present tense: Gareth serves, not served
quotationsa comma before the quotation; the closing mark, then the page citation in parentheses (the page number from your own copy), then the period
its / it’sits shows ownership; it’s means it is
then / thanthen tells when; than compares
their / there / they’retheir shows ownership; there names a place; they’re means they are

📌 Watch how
Elena’s paragraph
6th Grade Scholar

It is true that Launcelot is the greatest knight in arms. When King Arthur falls in battle, Launcelot will not let Sir Bors end the war with one stroke, and he very tenderly helps the king onto his own horse (page). Even Gawain, who has sworn to fight him, calls him the “flower of all noble knights” (page). A reader who admires Launcelot could say that no knight shows more courtesy. Yet Green measures a good knight by more than courtesy in war. Launcelot himself says he is not “worthy to wear” the sword in the floating stone (page), and the damsel who brings the news calls him the best only “of sinful men” (page). Gareth hides only his name, so that he can prove himself worthy by his deeds (page). For a whole year he serves in the kitchen without answering Sir Kay back. Mocked all along the road by Lady Linnet, he answers her courteously and keeps his promise. Launcelot’s greatness is real. Gareth’s goodness goes all the way through.

Where Elena writes (page), your own paragraph gives the page number from your copy.

Panel 2The Frame, and Draft2Revise the introduction and the conclusion of your essay
📌 Your outline
Introduction
It opens with a hook from the book.
It says the purpose: comparing two knights to answer “What makes a good knight?”
It gives one or two sentences of background on Green’s book.
It ends with the claim, which names both knights.
Conclusion
It restates the claim in fresh words.
It says what the comparison reveals about a good knight.
It ends on a moment or an idea, not a list.
📌 Watch how
Elena’s introduction and conclusion
6th Grade Scholar

Introduction. When a damsel tells Launcelot that he was the best knight in the world, he answers, “I knew well that I was never the best.” Roger Lancelyn Green’s King Arthur and His Knights of the Round Table retells the old stories of Camelot, and it keeps asking what makes a knight good. This essay compares Sir Launcelot and Sir Gareth to answer that question. Green suggests that Gareth is the better knight, because his goodness goes all the way through, while Launcelot’s greatness is strongest in battle.

Conclusion. Launcelot may be the greatest knight in arms, but Gareth is the better knight, because he is good in the kitchen as well as in the field. The comparison shows that Green measures a knight by more than skill: by patience when he is mocked, courtesy when he is insulted, and faithfulness to his word. In the end, the knight who asks only for meat and drink asks for the most: a chance to earn his place by his deeds.
